description: Bulgar-Turkic state on the middle Volga (c. 900–1236) that converted to Islam (922) and became a major node in the Eurasian fur trade connecting Scandinavia to the Islamic world; its destruction by the Mongols in 1236 eliminated this early Turkic-Islamic state but its population contributed to the later Tatar identity of the Kazan region.

temporal.notes: Islamic Volga trade polity; Mongol destruction.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Kotrag's Bulgars migrate to the Volga; khanate established.
Volga trade network matures; Islam adopted 922.
Height of commercial power; Ibn Fadlan visits 921–922.
Batu Khan's conquest; Volga Bulgaria absorbed into Golden Horde.

rise_factors.description: Bulgar Itil at the Volga bend was the key node between Baltic fur and amber trade and Abbasid silver via the Caspian.
Adoption of Islam in 922 under Almış connected Volga Bulgaria to the Islamic world's trading and diplomatic networks.
Furs, slaves, beeswax, and honey from the northern forest zone passed through Volga Bulgaria, generating exceptional transit revenues.

Volga Bulgaria's position on the Volga-Kama river junction made it the primary entrepôt for northern fur trade, sable, ermine, beaver, connecting Baltic, Scandinavian, and Islamic markets from the 9th century.
Tsar Almish's conversion to Islam in 922 (documented by Ibn Fadlan) brought Volga Bulgaria into the Islamic trade network, attracting Abbasid and Samanid merchants and diplomatic recognition.

decline_factors.description: Mongol-Tatar armies under Batu and Subutai conquered Volga Bulgaria in 1236–1241 after an earlier probe in 1223–1224.
Mongol destruction of the Bulgar city and forced incorporation into the Golden Horde eliminated Volga Bulgaria as a political entity.
Warfare and forced population movement devastated the Volga Bulgarian population.

Mongol forces under Batu Khan destroyed Volga Bulgaria's capital Bilär in 1236, massacring the population and incorporating the territory into the Golden Horde, ending the state's independent existence.
The surviving Bulgar population was absorbed into the Golden Horde's multi-ethnic structure; their descendants contributed to the formation of the Khanate of Kazan after the Horde's fragmentation.
